title: Muller's-ratchet recombination: two error-riddled copies make one clean page
idea: Sexual recombination breaks Muller's ratchet by mixing genomes with different mutations; store each page twice in very cheap cells with only an 8-bit CRC per 8-byte chunk (detect, not correct), assemble reads chunk by chunk from whichever copy passes, rewrite the failing chunk, and fall back to a rare third copy on double hits.
why: Cost per GB: replaces correction logic with detection plus duplication, so media at raw BER ~1e-5 (a 100x-cheaper class) works at ~2.25x bit overhead with trivially cheap decode.

title: Seismic base isolation: grounded shield rail buried between wordlines
idea: Base isolation decouples a building from ground shaking. A thin grounded TiN or doped-poly rail is buried in the isolation trench between adjacent buried wordlines. It terminates the fringing fields and collects the electrons injected by the aggressor before they reach the victim storage-node junctions.
why: It could raise the row-hammer threshold about 10x, from ~1k to ~10k ACTs (fact 9), removing most counter area and RFM bandwidth. The cost is a small increase in pitch.

title: Defect-aware coset coding makes weak cells store their safe value
idea: Ideal: defects that happen to store the right value. Closest: the encoder knows each row's weak-cell positions from a BIST map and, using Kuznetsov-Tsybakov coding for memories with defects, picks one of several coset encodings so every weak cell holds the value it decays toward; a few index bits per block replace remapping.
why: Fact 3: neutralizes known tail cells with ~2-4% overhead and no spare rows, using simple 180 nm logic.

title: Substitute laser fuse repair with in-field cuckoo remap in HBM base die
idea: Replace one-shot fuse row repair with a 64-byte-granular cuckoo-hash remap table in the HBM logic base die, backed by spare rows, that is rewritten in the field whenever ECC sees a recurring error, so dies with 10x more defects than today's repair budget still ship.
why: HBM yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6): recovering half of the lost stacks raises effective HBM supply ~10-15% with no new wafers.

title: Drum clock-track revival: leaky canary columns time each subarray's refresh
idea: Magnetic drums carried a dedicated clock track that timed everything else on the drum. Each subarray gets one canary column of cells built deliberately at the leaky tail (shorter gate, extra junction implant) that is rewritten at every refresh; the subarray is refreshed only when canaries start failing sensing, so the interval tracks local temperature, voltage and aging instead of a fixed 64 ms.
why: Refresh energy (fact 3): most subarrays most of the time could run 3-8x longer intervals; area ~0.2%.

title: Zn: indium-free zinc-tin-oxide TFT layer hosts ECC logic above array
idea: Fabricate a BEOL ZnSnO thin-film-transistor logic layer (Zn and Sn are abundant; no In or Ga) over the cell array to hold on-die ECC syndrome decoders and row/column repair muxes, wired down by vias to local sense amps.
why: Moves reliability logic out of the ~49% periphery (fact 7) so stronger on-die ECC costs no die area; ~3-5% die shrink or 2x ECC strength at equal area.

title: Bit-significance routing across strong and derated memory pools
idea: Box [medium: recycled or derated DRAM dies | access: standard | sense: standard | integration: CXL memory pool | substrate: reclaimed DIMMs | fab: legacy]. A CXL controller bit-slices bf16/fp8 tensors so sign and exponent bits land in a chipkill-protected pool while low mantissa bits land in end-of-life or out-of-spec dies with no ECC and 4x relaxed refresh.
why: Supply: returns retired and downbinned DRAM to service; ~30-50% of AI memory capacity can tolerate flips with <1% accuracy impact.

title: Cu: copper cold-plate DIMM sleeves buy 4x longer refresh
idea: A machined, brazed copper sleeve plumbed into the server's existing liquid loop holds DRAM packages below 45 C; after a per-module retention screen, BIOS tables set tREFI 2-4x longer. CNC and brazing fit a 10-person shop.
why: Retention roughly doubles per 10 C; recovers much of the 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth lost to refresh (fact 3).

title: Minify hydrogen with getter-laced glass to freeze oxide-TFT drift
idea: Embed hydrogen-getter layers (Ti- or Pd-alloy films or getter-doped glass) in or on the substrate to absorb hydrogen that diffuses into IGZO channels and drives threshold drift and leakage growth.
why: Fact 3 and self-healing: stabilizes oxide-TFT leakage over life, keeping retention near day-one values and cutting aging guardbands.

title: Child writes bigger where paper is rough: quality-adaptive bits per cell
idea: A child writes bigger on bumpy paper: the controller reads a per-region print-quality map (device sigma, leakage) for a printed memory foil and configures each region for 2 bits/cell where devices are tight, 1 bit/cell where they are average, and one bit across two ganged cells where they are poor, exposing whatever capacity results.
why: Variation becomes a capacity variable instead of a yield loss: nothing is scrapped, and average density can beat a worst-case design by ~1.5x.

title: Eliminate controller refresh timers: per-row canary cells trigger refresh
idea: Add one deliberately weakened canary cell to each row (smaller capacitor, leakier transistor) and write it to '1' at every restore. A low-power background sense polls the canaries, and only rows whose canary has decayed get refreshed, so refresh tracks actual temperature and leakage.
why: Most rows retain data for seconds; demand-driven refresh could cut refresh count ~5-10x and the bandwidth loss (fact 3) in proportion, with a self-calibrating guard-band.

title: Sacrificial canary cells trigger refresh only when needed
idea: Worse: refresh every row at the worst-case 64 ms forever, blind to real temperature and aging. Flip: plant ~0.1% deliberately weakened canary cells (half-depth capacitor, leakier junction) in every subarray; a tiny comparator polls them and refreshes that subarray only when canaries start to decay, so refresh tracks actual physics instead of a datasheet guardband.
why: Fact 3 refresh tax: typical retention is 10-100x the 64 ms spec, so canary-paced refresh can cut refresh energy/bandwidth loss 4-10x, and weaker main cells can ship because the canary tracks their real decay.

title: Antiferromagnetic memory's weak readout fixed with Mn3Sn tunnel junctions
idea: CuMnAs electrically switched antiferromagnetic memory stalled because its readout signal (anisotropic magnetoresistance ~0.1%) was too weak. Fix: use noncollinear antiferromagnets such as Mn3Sn or Mn3Pt, whose momentum-space spin splitting yields large tunneling magnetoresistance in an all-antiferromagnet tunnel junction, while keeping spin-orbit-torque switching.
why: Nonvolatile and zero refresh, with no stray fields, so neighbor disturb (a row-hammer analogue) and external-field upsets vanish; picosecond-scale dynamics.

title: Reed's 1954 majority-logic decoder built into the sense-amp stripe
idea: Irving Reed decoded Reed-Muller codes with one layer of parity checks feeding majority gates, with no iterative algebra. Weak subarrays use a one-step majority-logic-decodable (273,191) difference-set code whose XOR checks and majority votes form a single gate layer beside the column multiplexer, correcting 8 random errors per access in ~1 ns with no syndrome tables.
why: Weaker cells acceptable (facts 1, 3): tolerates raw BER ~1e-4 instead of ~1e-9 without a latency penalty, so Cs can drop ~30% or refresh stretch ~8x in those subarrays; ~40% parity there, applied only where cells are weak.

title: Panel-fab DRAM on Gen-8.5 glass with oxide-TFT access
idea: Po: memory printed like television screens. Idle flat-panel lines pattern 1T1C arrays on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass with oxide TFTs at sub-micron imprint rules; TFT variability gives ~1% BER, and the panels are diced into a near-DRAM capacity tier bonded to a logic decoder.
why: Capital: panel area costs ~100x less per m^2 than wafer area; ~$2-4/GB only if ~0.5 um rules are reached, with latency at the slow edge of DRAM-class (~100 ns+).

title: Bit-flip-hardened training so AI memory runs at relaxed refresh
idea: Ideal: the application does not care about memory errors. Closest: train and fine-tune models with injected bit-flip noise matching a 1e-6 raw BER profile, protect only optimizer state and index tensors with CRC, then deploy weights and activations in DRAM running at 8x the normal refresh interval.
why: Fact 3: AI memory (the main demand driver) gets ~80% lower refresh energy and ~10% more bandwidth with <0.1% accuracy loss.

title: Matrix checksums replace DRAM ECC for AI weights
idea: Inverts 'memory must protect itself': weight matrices carry row and column checksum vectors (algorithm-based fault tolerance); the GEMM kernel verifies output checksums and corrects single weight-tile errors, so HBM holding weights runs without on-die ECC or with relaxed refresh.
why: Reclaims the ~12% ECC area and bandwidth in HBM (fact 6) and tolerates higher raw BER for <2% compute overhead.

title: Zero refresh budget: rewrites of training tensors serve as refresh
idea: Imposed limit: the DRAM may spend zero cycles on refresh. The controller keeps a 2-bit last-written epoch per row, and the training runtime guarantees every activation, gradient and KV buffer is rewritten each step (<20 ms). Rows written within tRET are never refreshed; only a small long-lived bank group holding weights and optimizer state keeps conventional refresh.
why: Fact 3: refresh is 16-33% of idle power and 10-20% of bandwidth. In training, 70-90% of rows are short-lived, so most refresh energy and bandwidth loss disappear.

title: E8 lattice coding packs 3 bits/cell in noisy gain cells
idea: Slicing each multilevel cell independently is a cubic lattice and wastes ~3 dB of packing gain. Group 8 gain cells and map 24 bits onto E8 lattice points, the densest packing in 8D, decodable with a few hundred gates. The Voronoi decision regions give 1.5-3 dB more margin against drift.
why: Density: 2 to 3 bits/cell (+50%) with the same capacitorless cells and retention drift.

title: Tetris placement: compressed payload shifted so slack lands on weak bits
idea: Lines are compressed (BDI/FPC); the controller keeps a per-row weak-bit mask and rotates/offsets the compressed payload inside the 64 B line so known-weak or stuck positions fall into padding, recorded by a 3-6 bit shift field - PCM stuck-at masking ported to DRAM retention tails.
why: ~40% of lines become immune to known weak cells with no extra parity, permitting longer refresh or acceptance of cheaper, leakier dies.

title: Humbucker twin-cell mode on commodity DRAM for critical data
idea: Adapted from humbucking guitar pickups that pair two opposite-polarity coils to cancel hum: the controller uses the simultaneous multi-row activation already demonstrated on off-the-shelf DDR chips to write a row and its complement into a paired row on the opposite bitline side, so the sense amp sees a differential signal; critical pages (kernel, page tables, keys) run in this twin mode at half capacity.
why: Retention and row hammer (facts 3, 9): differential twin cells give ~2x signal and common-mode disturbance rejection, potentially extending retention 10x+ and resisting hammering for the few percent of memory that needs it, with no new silicon.

title: IBM 650 SOAP-style placement puts tolerant tensors in the hottest dies
idea: The IBM 650's SOAP assembler placed each instruction where the rotating drum would deliver it soonest. A placement compiler does the same with heat: from a thermal map of the HBM stack (top and centre dies run hottest) it places error-tolerant data (KV cache, activations, gradients) in the hottest banks with relaxed refresh and critical data (optimizer state, page tables) in the coolest, most protected banks.
why: Water: the stack's allowed average temperature rises ~10-15 C because only tolerant data sit in hot spots, enabling warm-water dry cooling without evaporation (>10x less facility water); refresh energy -30%.

title: Triple-row activation gives free analog majority voting
idea: Inverts 'only one row opens at a time': critical data (page tables, kernel, model metadata) is written into three rows of one subarray; a read opens all three at once so charge sharing makes the sense amp resolve the majority, giving TMR voting in a single access with no logic.
why: Hammer- and retention-proof storage (facts 3, 9) for the ~1% of data whose corruption is catastrophic, with no added latency.

title: Rosetta stone: dual-technology copies with uncorrelated hot failure modes
idea: Critical data (page tables, ECC metadata, kernel) is written in two 'scripts': once in 1T1C DRAM and once in an oxide-channel gain-cell region whose temperature failure mechanism differs, with per-copy ECC arbitrating any mismatch.
why: At 125 C mirrored copies fail together by the same mechanism; diversity gives orders-lower silent corruption for <2% capacity, letting the bulk run thinner margins for 10 years.

title: Triple-row majority refresh votes critical data clean in-DRAM
idea: Po: the sense amp is the judge. Page tables, kernel text and model metadata are kept as three copies in one subarray; at refresh the DRAM does a triple-row activation whose charge sharing yields the bitwise majority, written back to all three rows, so scrubbing happens with no data movement.
why: Protecting the few critical bytes in-array lets the bulk of the device run looser refresh/ECC; scrub energy ~100x lower than reading out to the controller.

title: Flikker's annotation burden removed by hardware bit-plane splitting of tensors
idea: Flikker-style approximate refresh failed because programmers had to hand-mark non-critical data. Fix: the memory controller transposes words on pages whose dtype (bf16/fp8/int8) is known from the ML allocator, so sign/exponent bits land in fully refreshed rows while low mantissa bits land in rows refreshed 16x less often that tolerate ~1e-4 BER.
why: ~50-60% of AI tensor bits move to relaxed rows: ~45% refresh energy cut (fact 3) and rows of weaker cells become sellable, with negligible accuracy loss.

title: Three-tier charge-summing majority vote on a shared vertical bitline
idea: Combine triple modular redundancy with charge sharing: three cheap stacked oxide-TFT/capacitor tiers on one vertical bitline are written together and read by opening all three gates at once, so the bitline sees the analog sum and one fully leaked or shorted cell cannot flip the bit. Buildable in a university nanofab: three sequential low-temperature IGZO/MIM tiers.
why: No manufacturable 3D cell (fact 2): makes low-yield, leaky tiers acceptable because each bit tolerates a bad tier, enabling cheap BEOL stacking despite 3x cells.

title: Railway sidings: on-die hot-row SRAM cache absorbs hammering
idea: Adapted from rail yards that pull a heavily used train onto a siding to keep the main line clear: each bank has a 16-entry row-wide SRAM siding; when a row's approximate activation count (Misra-Gries tracker) crosses ~200, the row is copied into the siding and served from SRAM until it cools, so the physical row stops toggling.
why: Row hammer (fact 9) and activation energy (fact 8): the aggressor physically stops activating, eliminating victim-refresh storms and saving ~1 nJ per avoided activation on hot rows, for ~1% die area.

title: SAQP pitch-walk classes get their own refresh and ECC
idea: No EUV: self-aligned quadruple patterning on DUV produces systematic alpha/beta/gamma line-width classes. Scale shift (litho systematics -> refresh scheduling): tag each row by its spacer class at design time and run separate refresh intervals and ECC strengths per class rather than guard-banding all rows to the worst class.
why: Recovers ~20-40% of refresh energy and lets multi-patterning replace EUV despite its CD variation.

title: Hydra conveyor: charge shifts continuously up vertical CCD strings
idea: Hydra tissue flows endlessly from body column to tentacles and is shed; use a 3D-NAND vertical string as a charge-coupled shift register, stepping charge packets along 200+ gate layers and regenerating them at a sense amp at the top of each loop, so no packet sits long enough to leak and transfer errors are reset at every regeneration.
why: Cost per GB: NAND-fab cost structure (~100x cheaper per bit), no capacitor, refresh replaced by circulation itself; trade is serial access (~us to first byte), fit for capacity tiers and streaming.

title: Double-sampling sense amps catch late-resolving bits at low voltage
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: Razor-style dual-sample sense with shadow latch | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Each sense amp latches at a nominal time and again ~1.5 ns later; a disagreement marks a slowly resolving low-signal bit, which is corrected from the shadow sample and its row queued for restore at higher voltage.
why: Constraint: removes the worst-case voltage guard band (VARY ~1 V to ~0.35 V, ~8x CV^2); errors are detected in situ without extra code bits.

title: Spare subarray swap triggered by ECC error-trend detection
idea: Rule: big defects must be fixable in place. Each bank holds one spare subarray (~1/64). When ECC logs show a subarray's error rate trending upward (for example, a failing sense-amp stripe), it is copied into the spare with in-DRAM bulk row copy and remapped live.
why: Repairs large-area defects that spare rows cannot cover at ~1.5% area, so fewer modules are retired.

title: Program-verify writes tolerate higher-resistance NiSi contacts
idea: Worse: replace cobalt and tungsten contacts with nickel silicide and watch write failures rise from higher contact resistance. Flip: give DRAM a NAND-style write-verify loop: after restore, the sense amp re-checks the bit against a tightened reference and re-pulses only failing columns, so marginal-resistance contacts no longer cause silent errors.
why: Removes Co and W from contacts while tolerating 2-3x contact-resistance spread; ~1-3% write latency cost, paid only on retries.

title: Negative-capacitance HZO access gate removes the wordline pump
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: negative-capacitance FET with matched HZO gate layer | sense: standard | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: ALD]. A capacitance-matched ferroelectric layer gives the access transistor ~40 mV/decade subthreshold swing, so it reaches today's off-leakage at 0 V and today's on-current at ~1.1 V instead of a ~3 V pumped wordline, pushing the leakage tail down by orders of magnitude.
why: Constraint: wordline CV^2 ~7x lower and no ~3x pump loss, >10x on the wordline path; Fact 3: refresh drops with the tail.

title: Conveyor memory: data circulates so refresh and scrub are inherent
idea: Ideal: memory that is always being read, so always fresh and always checked. Closest: a 180 nm shift-loop DRAM in which every row's data circulates through a sense-and-ECC station every few milliseconds, so refresh and scrubbing happen as a side effect of motion, with many short loops keeping average access near 100 ns.
why: Fact 3: no separate refresh scheduling and errors are corrected before they accumulate; suits a bulk refresh-tolerant tier.

title: Watertight-bulkhead subarrays with current-limit breakers contain metal shorts
idea: Ships survive hull breaches through watertight bulkheads; since argon-free metallisation (N2-reactive or CVD/ALD-only with no Ar PVD) can raise particle and short rates, give each subarray its own power and wordline-pump domain behind a self-resetting current-limit switch, so one short is isolated and the mat is retired instead of sinking the die.
why: Turns die-killing shorts into a loss of 1/N capacity, keeping rare-gas-free metallisation yield-viable; partially good dies ship at a lower density grade.

title: Hundred-electron storage nodes read by single-electron electrometers
idea: Box [medium: ~100-electron Si quantum-dot node | access: Si nanowire gate | sense: single-electron transistor electrometer | integration: monolithic | substrate: SOI | fab: e-beam or DSA]. Each bit is ~100 electrons sensed by a capacitively coupled SET that resolves single electrons, stored as 3-way repetition with Poisson-aware soft decoding that treats leakage as counting noise.
why: Constraint: stored charge ~16 aC versus ~5 fC, so access energy can fall >100x; Fact 1: removes the capacitor entirely.

title: Unrepaired weak cells kept as live refresh-rate governors
idea: TRIZ #22 Blessing in disguise: instead of repairing every weak cell, ~1,000 known-weak cells per bank stay in place holding a known pattern; checking them each window measures real leakage (temperature, aging, radiation) and sets refresh just above their failure point.
why: Replaces worst-case 64/32 ms guardbands with measured margin: ~2-4x fewer refreshes at typical temperatures, and repair resources are saved for clusters.

title: Z-channel coding lets a one be stored at eighth charge
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: asymmetric reference near the empty level | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: DUV]. Because DRAM charge only leaks away (1->0), the sense reference sits just above empty with a small guard band and '1' is written at ~0.35 V; the rare 1->0 losses are fixed by a unidirectional Bose-Lin code needing ~half the check bits of symmetric BCH.
why: Constraint: write/restore charge and bitline swing fall ~8-10x; the code matches the physics of the error channel.

title: Eliminate parallel wordline adjacency: rotate alternate 3D tiers 90 degrees
idea: In stacked 3D DRAM, run wordlines in X on odd tiers and in Y on even tiers, so vertically adjacent wordlines cross at points instead of running in parallel. Each in-tier wordline pair is separated by a shield line that doubles as the plate.
why: Hammer coupling scales with shared parallel length; crossing geometry could cut vertical aggressor coupling >10x, removing a key 3D row hammer threat (facts 2, 9).

title: PARA revived with sacrificial hammer-canary cells between rows
idea: PARA (probabilistic adjacent-row activation) was never adopted because at ~1k-ACT thresholds its trigger probability must be so high that blind neighbor refreshes eat bandwidth. Fix: place a strip of deliberately hammer-sensitive canary cells (thinner isolation, smaller Cs) along each wordline pair, read through a cheap dedicated sense line, and refresh neighbors only when a canary has physically flipped.
why: Mitigation triggered by physical evidence instead of dice rolls: ~5-10x fewer mitigation refreshes than PARA at equal safety, recovering ~3-8% bandwidth at 1k-ACT thresholds (fact 9).

title: SSD-controller playbook: 28nm CXL controller with page-level LDPC
idea: Adapted from NAND flash, which became cheap by pairing weak cells with smart controllers: a 28 nm CXL memory controller built in existing mature logic fabs applies 4 KB-codeword LDPC, with an on-chip SRAM write-combining buffer for read-modify-write, to unmodified commodity or lower-grade DRAM, exposing a byte-addressable device that tolerates raw BER ~1e-4.
why: Supply and cost per bit (facts 3, 4): operators can buy dies that fail JEDEC retention or speed bins at deep discounts and run them at 4-8x longer refresh; costs ~3% parity and ~50-100 ns added latency, acceptable for a CXL tier, with zero new fab capacity.

title: Food use-by dates: refresh-free perishable memory for short-lived data
idea: Adapted from perishable-food logistics, which ships milk faster than its shelf life instead of preserving it: a 28 nm logic-compatible 2T/3T gain-cell memory built in existing mature fabs never refreshes; allocations carry an expiry timestamp shorter than the measured retention, and the runtime places only short-lived data (activations, gradient buckets, network buffers) there, reallocating before expiry.
why: Refresh energy and capacity (fact 3): much of the AI working set lives microseconds to milliseconds; serving it from refresh-free trailing-node memory removes refresh cost and offloads leading-edge DRAM.

title: No new process step: wordline microheaters anneal leakage traps
idea: Imposed limit: the leakage tail must improve without adding fab steps. Existing wordline and dummy-gate conductors are driven as resistive heaters in maintenance windows (about 1 s pulses heating locally to ~250 C), passivating hydrogen-related interface traps and resetting variable-retention-time defects in the array.
why: Fact 3: shrinking the ≤13 fA tail could let the refresh interval stretch ~4x, plus self-healing of aging-induced leakage over the product's life.

title: Recommender hot rows: replicate embedding rows across banks to dilute activations
idea: Recommendation models with Zipf-skewed embedding lookups hit a few rows millions of times per second. The runtime keeps per-row activation counts in a Misra-Gries sketch and replicates the hottest rows into 4-8 banks, round-robining reads so no physical row crosses the hammer threshold. Bank parallelism also raises bandwidth.
why: Workload-driven hammering is what forces conservative cells. Dilution keeps per-row activations under ~1k for ~0.1% capacity overhead (fact 9).

title: Retention-signature die matching when assembling stacks
idea: No EUV: mature DUV dies have wider retention spread. Scale shift (die test data -> package assembly): sort known-good dies into retention-signature bins and stack only matched dies, so each stack runs at its own refresh rate instead of the worst die's in a random mix; outlier dies go to high-refresh SKUs.
why: Cuts stack refresh overhead ~2x and raises usable yield of wide-spread DUV dies.

title: Core-memory inhibit winding revived as anti-hammer neighbour counter-pulse
idea: Coincident-current core planes drove an 'inhibit' current through cores that must not switch, cancelling the half-select field. Each time a wordline rises, the drivers of its two physical neighbours apply a brief matched negative counter-pulse (~-0.3 V for the rise time) that cancels the capacitive kick and suppresses electron injection from the aggressor channel into neighbouring storage nodes, the mechanisms behind hammer flips.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): aims to push the flip threshold from ~1k to 10k+ activations, cutting mitigation refresh and counter overhead; costs ~5% extra wordline-driver energy.

title: Seismic base-isolation shield lines buried between wordlines
idea: Adapted from base-isolated buildings that decouple a structure from ground shaking: insert a grounded buried shield line (a dummy recessed gate held at slight negative bias) between every pair of active buried wordlines, so aggressor wordline swings and hot electrons injected into the substrate are absorbed by the shield rather than the victim storage node.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): blocks both electrostatic coupling and trap-assisted charge pumping, potentially raising flip thresholds 10x+ at ~15-25% array-area cost (6F2 to ~7.5F2), trading density for deleting counters, RFM and victim-refresh overhead.

title: One end-to-end code replaces on-die ECC, link CRC, host ECC
idea: DDR5 pays separately for on-die SEC (6.25%), link CRC and host SECDED/chipkill. Shannon does not care where the noise enters. Encode once at the host with one long code, store it raw, and decode at the host using soft information from the link.
why: Periphery/overhead (fact 7): recovers ~6% die area and energy while correcting more errors.

title: Camera hot-pixel map: cell-level defect substitution table on die
idea: Adapted from CMOS image sensors, which ship with hundreds of dead pixels mapped out and patched in the ISP instead of scrapping the sensor: retention-weak and stuck cells found at test or in the field are recorded as compressed (row, column) entries in a small table on the logic base die, and a substitution engine overwrites those exact bit positions on every read with bits held in the table's own SRAM.
why: Yield and repair cost (facts 3, 7): per-cell substitution handles a 1e-6 weak-cell density at ~0.3% area instead of ~3-5% row/column redundancy, and lets fabs relax capacitor targets because the worst 1-ppm tail is handled individually.

title: Fractional-reserve parity: one XOR row backs many detection-only rows
idea: Banks hold reserves for only a fraction of deposits because withdrawals are rare. Each line keeps only a detection CRC-8. One XOR parity row in another bank backs each group of 32 rows. On a detected error, the line is rebuilt from the other 31 plus parity on a slow path. A controller write cache coalesces the parity read-modify-writes.
why: ECC storage overhead falls from 12.5% to ~3-6% while still correcting whole-line errors (cost per bit). It can be implemented in FPGA controller logic.

title: Geneticist's double helix: complementary bits printed on both foil faces
idea: DNA stores every base twice as complementary strands: each memory cell is printed on the front of the foil and its complement on the back (roll-to-roll double-sided printing with laser through-foil vias), read differentially, and any non-complementary pair is flagged and resolved in favor of the strand with the larger margin from midpoint.
why: Differential sensing doubles the signal, so weaker printed devices pass, and damage on one face (scratch, delamination, humidity) becomes detectable and correctable without ECC logic.

title: Mat parity row catches whole-row hammer bursts
idea: Inverts 'each word is corrected independently': every 512-row subarray dedicates one row to the XOR of all its rows, kept current on writes by in-array XOR; a row wiped by a hammer burst or wordline fault is rebuilt from the parity row and its siblings.
why: Converts row-hammer bursts (fact 9) and wordline failures from uncorrectable to correctable at ~0.2% capacity overhead.

title: Origami fold: subarray product code repairs whole-row hammer bursts
idea: Fold each subarray into a 2D grid: per-line ECC along rows plus one XOR parity row per 64 rows, kept current on writes via in-DRAM bitwise row operations or buffer-die read-modify-write, so a row riddled with hammer flips is rebuilt from the column parity as an erasure.
why: Fact 9: turns catastrophic multi-bit row-hammer and whole-row failures into correctable erasures at ~1.6% capacity, allowing relaxed hammer thresholds and fewer mitigation refreshes.

title: Training-cluster checkpoints replace ECC for bulk activations
idea: Scale jump (bit -> datacenter job): large training runs already checkpoint every few minutes, so activation and optimizer memory on non-ECC, denser, cheaper DRAM accepts silent-error risk. Cross-replica gradient checksums detect corruption and the job rolls back.
why: Recovers the ~12.5% ECC capacity and lets accelerators use lower-binned parts; converts reliability into a time-rollback budget.

title: Penguin huddle: rotate long-lived data through stack thermal zones
idea: Penguins rotate between the cold edge and warm center; in a 3D stack or multi-die module the controller tracks per-die temperature and periodically migrates long-lived pages so no data and no die sits in the hottest 125 C zone continuously.
why: Hotspot dies age and leak fastest; equalizing dose cuts worst-case 10-year Arrhenius exposure ~2x and lets cooler dies run lower refresh.

title: Villari magnetostrictive sensors map TSV stress for zone-specific refresh
idea: Effect: inverse magnetostriction (Villari). FeGa thin-film stripes whose permeability changes with mechanical stress, read inductively, ring the TSV clusters in HBM core dies and report local stress during warpage and thermal cycling; the controller maps stress-induced (piezoresistive) leakage to zone-specific refresh rates instead of a die-wide guard band.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): measured stress lets designers narrow conservative TSV keep-out zones (recovering ~2-5% die area) and drops stress-driven refresh guard bands.

title: Slow-edge two-level wordline precharge stops trap charge pumping
idea: One hammer mechanism is charge pumping: each ACT/PRE swing fills and empties interface traps under the aggressor or passing gate, emitting electrons toward the victim. Pumped charge per cycle falls when the falling edge is slower than trap emission time. A two-step precharge with a ramped edge (~ns) keeps trap occupancy near equilibrium.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): targets the pumping component, aiming for >5x higher ACT threshold and less TRR overhead.

title: Negative counter-pulse on neighbor wordlines cancels hammer electrons
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight: after each aggressor precharge, the two adjacent wordlines are driven ~0.3 V more negative for ~2 ns, creating a counter-field that sweeps electrons injected from the aggressor channel back before they reach victim storage nodes.
why: Fact 9 row hammer (~1k activations): if migrating charge dominates, the flip threshold could rise 5-10x with no counters, costing only a local pump and driver timing.

title: Kirchhoff current-sum checksum scrubs rows inside the array
idea: Effect: Kirchhoff current summation. During refresh, the restored sense-amp outputs of each column group drive equal unit currents onto a shared analog sum line, so the total current encodes the group's Hamming weight; a comparator checks it against a weight value stored in spare cells at write time. Only rows whose weight changed are shipped to the ECC engine for correction.
why: Patrol scrub moves entire rows to the controller: in-array detection makes frequent scrubbing nearly free (~10x less scrub energy and zero channel bandwidth), so weaker-retention cells can be tolerated by scrubbing more often.

title: Minify protection for regenerable data: CRC-detect, then recompute
idea: Classify data as regenerable (activations, KV cache, decompressed copies, file cache) and store it with only an 8-bit CRC per 512 bits. On a mismatch the runtime recomputes or re-fetches it from the source instead of correcting it.
why: Facts 3 and 4: frees most side-band ECC bits for capacity (+~10%) and lets regenerable data sit in weaker or slower-refreshed bins.

title: Constant-bias shield line between adjacent buried wordlines
idea: TRIZ #12 Equipotentiality: a narrow buried line held at a fixed negative potential sits between neighboring wordlines where the passing gate used to face the storage node, so the victim never sees the aggressor's 3 V swing or its trap-mediated electron flow.
why: Targets the passing-gate path behind the ~1k hammer threshold, aiming at 10x higher thresholds and lower GIDL for ~6F2 to 6.5F2 area.

title: High-pressure deuterium anneal passivates leakage-tail traps
idea: Ideal: an access transistor with zero interface traps. Closest: finish wafers with a high-pressure (5-20 atm) deuterium furnace anneal, a mid-1990s finding, because Si-D bonds resist thermal and hot-carrier breakage far better than Si-H, so trap-assisted junction leakage and VRT cells are passivated more completely and stay passivated.
why: Fact 3: possibly 2-5x fewer tail cells and longer refresh intervals using existing furnaces.

title: Corrected-error-rate feedback drives each bank to its own Vmin
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: standard with per-bank VARY/VPP regulators | integration: monolithic | substrate: bulk | fab: existing]. An on-die loop lowers each bank's VARY and VPP in 10 mV steps until the ECC-corrected error rate hits a target such as 1 per 1e9 bits, and raises them on temperature rise or error bursts, removing worst-silicon, worst-temperature and end-of-life guard bands.
why: Constraint: typical banks settle near 0.4-0.5 V versus the 1 V spec (~4-6x CV^2), and VPP scaling brings the wordline path to ~8-10x; reliability is a measured, regulated quantity.

title: Federal reliability-graded memory standard creates demand for DUV parts
idea: No EUV: a U.S. procurement standard defines 'graded memory' (module-level ECC plus row retirement plus telemetry) so federal and hyperscale buyers can buy DUV-made, weaker-cell DRAM at full qualification. Policy shifts demand toward non-EUV domestic supply.
why: Creates a guaranteed market that de-risks new U.S. DUV DRAM fabs (US share now ~1-2%).

title: Magnify ECC scope to the rack: erasure-coded CXL memory pools
idea: Stripe CXL-pooled memory with a 10+2 Reed-Solomon code across separate memory modules, so a dead chip or module is rebuilt rather than lost. Individual DRAM dies drop on-die ECC and ship with relaxed specs.
why: Facts 4 and 7: removes ~6-12% of on-die ECC area and accepts lower-grade dies; pool-level parity replaces per-die overhead and lifts usable supply.

title: U.S. reliability-broker buffer remediates sub-spec domestic DRAM dies
idea: TRIZ #24 Intermediary: a CXL/DIMM buffer chip fabbed on a U.S. mature logic line (12-22 nm class in New York) runs a strong LDPC code plus row remap over dies from U.S. DRAM fabs that fail JEDEC retention or hammer bins, and the module ships as spec-compliant.
why: Turns 5-15% of domestic wafer output now scrapped or downbinned into sellable capacity through an all-U.S. chain; ~10% lower cost per usable bit.

title: Crossbar Inc. ReRAM stuck faults self-healed by ECC-triggered reforming
idea: Crossbar Inc. and other ReRAM ventures lost DRAM-class ambitions to stuck-at-set/reset cells that accumulate with cycling. Fix: when the decoder corrects the same bit twice, the controller fires a reverse-polarity 'reforming' pulse that dissolves the overgrown or ruptured filament and re-forms it, returning the cell to service instead of retiring it.
why: Nonvolatile and zero refresh; in-field self-healing extends usable endurance ~10x and tolerates cheaper, less uniform films.

title: Spun-yarn bits: one bit's charge summed across several tiers
idea: Yarn spins many weak fibres into a strong thread; store each bit on 3-4 small capacitors in successive tiers sharing one vertical bitline and fired together, so a single leaky transistor from low-temperature, rare-gas-free tier deposition only shaves a fraction of the signal.
why: Averaging suppresses the leakage tail (fact 3) roughly by the fibre count and sums Cs across tiers to beat the charge wall (fact 1) without high aspect ratio; trades per-tier density for many cheap tiers.

title: Catalyst-regeneration detrap pulses during refresh idle
idea: Refineries burn coke off catalysts to restore activity; because rare-gas-free cell and gate dielectrics (no argon plasma densification) start with more traps, apply periodic negative-bias 'regeneration' pulses on idle wordlines to empty the filled traps behind VRT and gate-induced drain leakage.
why: Holds the leakage tail near its fresh-state value over life (fact 3) so cheaper rare-gas-free dielectrics can qualify; target ~1.5x longer refresh period.

title: Shipping-container reliability shell for alt-fab memory dies
idea: Containerisation let any cargo ride any ship; define a standard CXL buffer-chip 'container' (strong symbol ECC, scrubbing, page retirement, refresh management) so dies from new rare-gas-free alt-fabs (NIL, DSA, interference litho, UV-LED lines) plug into servers interchangeably despite raw BER ~100x worse than DDR5.
why: Lets fabs with no neon or helium dependence sell bits immediately, expanding U.S.-manufacturable supply (scarcity, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Substitute hours of factory retention testing with in-field learning
idea: Ship dies with only basic test and fast-refresh guard bands; the controller profiles retention per row over the first weeks of service at real temperature and then relaxes refresh row by row.
why: Capital/test cost (fact 4): retention test is a large share of DRAM test time and tester capex; removing it cuts back-end cost ~5-10% and frees tester capacity for supply.

title: Disposable two-year DRAM tier for checkpointed AI clusters
idea: TRIZ #27 Cheap short-living objects: a U.S.-made memory SKU designed for 2-year service in AI training racks with frequent checkpoints skips long burn-in and 10-year aging guardbands, ships with in-field error telemetry, and is swapped and recycled like a consumable.
why: Less screening and guardband adds 5-10% sellable bits per wafer and cuts test cost, aimed at domestic cost per bit and capacity.

title: High-field leakage fingerprint screens tail cells in seconds
idea: Tail cells are single traps with field-enhanced (Poole-Frenkel/trap-assisted tunneling) emission, so their leakage climbs steeply with junction field while normal cells barely change. At sort, write '1', raise the plate/substrate bias for 10 ms and read back. Failing cells are the would-be 64 ms tail and get mapped for repair or binning.
why: Test capital/time: replaces hours of retention bake with seconds per die and yields a per-row retention map for relaxed refresh.

title: Hibernating bear: hot-triggered compaction parks cold pages in strong rows
idea: Above ~105 C the controller or OS compresses cold pages 2-3x, packs them into the strongest-retention subarrays, and turns refresh off for the emptied subarrays (partial-array self-refresh).
why: Refresh power at 125 C is 4-8x room temperature; refreshing ~40% of the array cuts hot refresh energy ~60% and lowers self-heating over 10 years.

title: Compression-funded strong ECC lets marginal dies pass
idea: Po: ECC bits that cost nothing. The controller compresses each 64 B line (base-delta or zero-run); most real lines free 8+ bytes, which hold a strong BCH code, while incompressible lines fall back to standard SECDED and are steered to the strongest rows.
why: Yield: dies with higher weak-cell counts, previously scrapped, can ship, raising usable output ~5-10% with no extra ECC chips.

title: $1-IoT free ECC: compress each line to make room for parity
idea: Cheap IoT and phone LPDDR has no ECC pins. The host controller compresses each 64 B line (base-delta, zero and FP-pattern schemes succeed on ~70-90% of lines) and stores a SEC-DED or BCH code in the freed bits, tracked by one marker bit per line in a small metadata table. Standard non-ECC x16 parts gain protection on most lines.
why: Brings ECC to billions of non-ECC devices without the 12.5% extra chips, so phone and IoT DRAM can tolerate weaker cells and longer refresh (fact 3).

title: Sn: tin-can preservation compresses cold pages to fund ECC
idea: The controller compresses cold pages (typically 1.5-2x) and fills the freed bits with a strong Reed-Solomon code in place, so these pages tolerate 8-16x relaxed refresh in a low-refresh region with no capacity loss. Firmware plus RTL.
why: Cuts refresh energy (fact 3) for the cold majority of memory and makes weak cells tolerable.

title: Eliminate TSVs and microbumps: memory tiers deposited directly on HBM base die
idea: Instead of thinning, TSV-drilling and bonding DRAM dies, deposit <=400 C memory tiers monolithically on the HBM logic base die and connect them with ordinary BEOL vias at ~1 um pitch. The stack has no bumps, underfill or die-to-die misalignment to fail.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (3x area per bit, 20-30% yield loss, fact 6) and bump fatigue under thermal cycling; via density is ~100x higher.

title: Inverted HBM stack puts logic base die beside the lid
idea: Rearrange the stack so the hot base/logic die sits on top against the heat spreader and the DRAM dies sit below next to the interposer, with signals using the same through-stack TSVs; DRAM layers leave the logic die's heat path and run ~8-12 C cooler.
why: Retention roughly doubles per ~10 C, so refresh rate and retention-tail failures halve, or weaker cells are accepted at the same refresh.

title: Microfluidic channels etched in U.S.-made stack base die
idea: TRIZ #29 Pneumatics/hydraulics: coolant microchannels are etched into the domestically fabbed logic base die and capped with a bonded silicon lid, so liquid flows directly under the stack and holds DRAM dies at 60 C or below instead of 85-95 C.
why: Retention roughly doubles per 10 C drop, so ~4x longer refresh and no hot 2x-refresh mode; retention-weak dies pass, raising U.S. stack yield.

title: Pioneer-probe convolutional coding lets HBM run hot on dry coolers
idea: Pioneer 9 (1968) used convolutional codes with sequential decoding to pull data out of very noisy channels. HBM pages are encoded along each burst with a rate-15/16 tail-biting convolutional code decoded by a pipelined Viterbi in the logic base die, tolerating raw BER ~1e-3 at 6% overhead, enough to run the stack at ~115 C at the standard refresh rate.
why: Water: HBM's 85-95 C limit is usually the binding thermal constraint on accelerators; raising it ~20 C lets facilities use dry coolers year-round instead of evaporative towers (>10x less water) and also absorbs the retention tail (fact 3).

title: Compress-then-protect: freed bits buy strong ECC at 0.4 V
idea: Box [medium: capacitor | access: planar | sense: low-swing | integration: codec on HBM/CXL logic base die | substrate: bulk | fab: existing]. Each 64 B line is compressed (base-delta or zero-run) to at most 40 B, and the freed 24 B hold strong BCH/LDPC parity so that region runs at 0.4 V; incompressible lines (~25%) go to a 1 V region.
why: Constraint: ~1.6x fewer bits moved times ~6x lower array CV^2 gives ~10x per useful bit; parity costs no capacity.

title: Farmer's rain barrel: printed supercapacitor film steadies array voltage
idea: A farmer stores rain for the dry spell: a roll-to-roll-printed thin-film supercapacitor (carbon electrodes with an ion-gel electrolyte, mF/cm2) is laminated under the DRAM package or on the HBM interposer backside, supplying the current spikes of refresh and activate bursts so VARY droop shrinks and the voltage guardband can be cut.
why: Fact 10 voltage floor: removing ~50-100 mV of droop guardband cuts CV2 energy ~10-15% and reduces burst-induced sense failures.

title: Retinal filling-in: panel-scale nanoimprinted memory tolerating dead pixels
idea: Nanoimprint 2T oxide-semiconductor gain cells at F~100 nm onto Gen-10.5 display glass (~9 m2 per sheet); like the brain filling in the blind spot and dead photoreceptors, a power-up scan builds a defect map and a long Reed-Solomon erasure code reconstructs dead cells, so 1-3% dead pixels from imprint particles are acceptable.
why: Cost per GB/capital: display TFT area costs ~$50-150/m2 vs ~$100k/m2 for DRAM wafers; ~2 TB/m2 per layer gives ~$0.05/GB, ~100x below 2026 DRAM, trading latency (~100-300 ns) and areal density.

title: Switchboard operator: roll-to-roll antifuse crossbar foil reroutes dead bumps
idea: A telephone operator patches calls around a dead line: a thin roll-to-roll-made interposer foil carrying a crossbar of printed antifuses sits between the memory stack's base die and the package; after assembly test, the controller fires antifuses to route signals from failed microbumps or TSV channels to spares.
why: Fact 6: HBM loses 20-30% of yield to stacking and TSV defects; rerouting after assembly could recover much of it without redesigning the stack.

title: SYN-cookie style epoch-keyed row scrambling against hammering
idea: Adapted from network security's stateless key rotation (SYN cookies, ASLR re-randomization): the DRAM die applies a keyed bijective permutation (a 4-round Feistel on row-address bits) between logical and physical rows inside each subarray and re-keys every epoch by migrating rows during refresh slots, so no attacker holds a fixed set of physical neighbors for more than one epoch.
why: Row hammer at ~1k activations (fact 9): turns deterministic double-sided attacks into random spraying, raising the effective per-victim threshold by roughly rows-per-subarray/2 without per-row counters, saving counter area and PRAC timing penalties.

title: Smart Refresh counters replaced by streaming sweep-coverage proofs
idea: Smart Refresh (skipping refresh for recently accessed rows) died because per-row timestamp counters cost area and gave no coverage guarantee. Fix: accelerators that stream every weight row each iteration order reads as a strict per-bank address sweep, so one sweep pointer plus a deadline timer proves every row was activated within tREFW; the refresh engine is disabled, and if the workload stalls past the deadline the region is marked stale and reloaded from its persistent copy.
why: Zero refresh power and zero refresh bandwidth loss (10-20%, fact 3) for weight-resident HBM.

title: Aviation regulator: certify printed memory by error class, not perfection
idea: An aviation certifier grades components by how they fail, not whether they fail: a JEDEC-style qualification ladder for printed and roll-to-roll memory (raw-BER class, fault-geometry class, drift class, required host ECC/redundancy profile), backed by a U.S. test lab funded under CHIPS, lets system makers design in imperfect printed tiers with guaranteed post-correction reliability.
why: Removes the qualification barrier that keeps cheap printed memory out of servers and opens a path for U.S. roll-to-roll memory manufacturing.

title: Triaxial-weave parity: row, column and diagonal threads catch clusters
idea: Triaxial fabrics weave threads at 0, 60 and 120 degrees so tears cannot run; overlay three interleaved parity families on each subarray mat (rows, columns, 60-degree diagonals), updated by on-die XOR trees at write-back, so a particle defect, a dead wordline segment or a hammered neighbourhood is located where three failing parity threads intersect and is corrected during scrub.
why: 2D clusters defeat on-die SEC; three-direction parity corrects them for ~3% overhead versus 6-12% for strong symbol codes, letting clustered-defect dies ship and absorbing hammer bursts (fact 9).

title: National open physics-of-failure testbed for capacitorless cells
idea: CHIPS/NIST funds a shared lab that runs standardized retention, disturb, endurance and VRT stresses on any capacitorless cell (gain, floating-body, volatile MRAM, domain-wall). It publishes raw distributions and activation-energy-based acceleration models.
why: U.S. manufacturability/time: each entrant's qualification shrinks from years and ~$50M to months.

title: Air gaps between buried wordlines cut hammer coupling
idea: TRIZ #31 Porous materials: a sacrificial carbon spacer between neighboring buried wordlines is ashed out through a pinch-off cap using U.S.-vendor deposition/etch tools, leaving an air gap (k=1) that weakens capacitive and field coupling from aggressor to victim.
why: Coupling capacitance drops ~40-50%; if hammer flips track coupling the threshold rises severalfold and wordline RC falls too, with domestic tools and chemicals.

title: Magnify grain size so each LTPS access transistor sits in one grain
idea: Use sequential lateral solidification or seeded laser crystallization on glass to grow polysilicon grains longer than each access or periphery transistor, so no channel contains a grain boundary, the main source of LTPS leakage and Vt spread.
why: Facts 3 and 7: tightens LTPS leakage tails by about an order of magnitude, making glass-based periphery and access devices reliable.

title: Bridge strain-gauge sentinels: deliberately weak canary cells gate refresh
idea: Adapted from structural health monitoring, where cheap gauges alarm before the bridge fails: each subarray includes a column of sentinel cells built with ~70% of nominal capacitor height (one extra trim step) so they leak first; a subarray is refreshed only when its sentinels begin to flip, checked for free during normal activations.
why: Refresh power (fact 3): most subarrays retain far longer than the 32/64 ms worst case; sentinel-gated refresh can cut refresh operations 3-6x at typical temperatures, with a margin tied to real local leakage and temperature.

title: One mask grows deliberately weak sentinel cells that call refresh
idea: Inverts 'refresh runs on a timer': the single added mask partially blocks the mold etch for a few sentinel cells per subarray so their capacitors are shorter and fail first; a sentinel flip, found by a cheap probe read, triggers refresh of only that subarray.
why: Refresh follows actual local temperature and leakage instead of worst-case 32/64 ms timers; ~50-75% refresh cut (fact 3).

title: Canary cells: deliberately weakened sentinels set per-subarray refresh
idea: Forced connection to the coal-mine canary: each subarray carries ~64 sentinel cells built with ~60% of normal Cs (truncated pillar or partial plate), written to '1' and sensed every window; their first failures set that subarray's refresh interval through a tiny on-die state machine instead of a global worst-case 32/64 ms.
why: Fact 3 refresh tax: typical subarrays run 4-8x longer intervals while the weakened canaries bound tail risk; ~60-75% less refresh energy and bandwidth loss.

title: Deliberately weakened canary cells set each subarray's refresh
idea: Po: memory that fails on purpose to warn you. Each subarray carries ~64 sentinel cells built with a thinned capacitor or an extra junction-leakage implant so they fail at ~0.6x the retention of the worst real cell; the in-DRAM scheduler slows refresh until canaries start to flip, then backs off one step.
why: Refresh (fact 3): each subarray runs at its true retention instead of the global worst case, ~2-4x fewer refreshes at normal temperatures.

title: Na: sodium-dosed sentinel capacitors forecast mat failure early
idea: Each mat carries a few SiN-encapsulated sentinel cells whose dielectric holds a controlled Na+ dose, so they leak and age ~10x faster under identical temperature and voltage; refresh logic polls them and tightens refresh or retires the mat as soon as sentinels start failing.
why: Turns retention-tail uncertainty (fact 3) into a measured early warning, so nominal refresh can run with less guardband (~1.5-2x longer tREFI) without risking silent errors.

title: Ga: gallium-tin liquid-metal contacts self-heal intermittent DIMM connectors
idea: An interposer with sealed microcups of Ga-Sn eutectic (In-free; gram quantities despite gallium's China concentration) replaces spring contacts; the liquid metal flows around fretting and oxide, eliminating intermittent connector faults that masquerade as memory errors and trigger DIMM pulls.
why: Many field 'memory failures' are connector or signal-integrity faults; avoiding needless replacement raises effective supply.

title: Al: Al2O3 negative charge passivates storage junction surfaces, solar-style
idea: Line STI sidewalls and the buried-wordline trench top near the storage node with ALD Al2O3, whose ~-5e12 cm^-2 fixed negative charge accumulates holes at the p-type surface and pushes the depletion region off the defective interface (the field-effect passivation used in PERC solar cells).
why: Suppresses surface-generation leakage, a major retention-tail contributor (fact 3), with abundant Al and existing ALD; target 2-5x tail reduction.

title: Goto's parametron revived: parametric bitline pumping senses tiny charges
idea: Eiichi Goto's 1954 parametron stored a bit as the phase of a parametrically pumped oscillation. Pump the bitline pair's MOS varactor at twice the sense frequency during sensing, so the cell's small charge seeds the phase of an oscillation that grows exponentially, with gain set by matched capacitors instead of threshold-mismatched latch transistors.
why: Capacitor charge wall and voltage floor (facts 1, 10): latch offset (~10-20 mV) dominates margin; parametric sensing could tolerate ~2x smaller signal, allowing Cs near 2.5 fF or longer retention.

title: Chaos engineering certifies software so memory specs can relax
idea: Adapted from Netflix-style chaos engineering, which injects failures in production until systems tolerate them: a hypervisor-level injector flips random bits in tagged memory regions at controlled rates, and applications that pass sustained injection at BER ~1e-7 are certified to run on relaxed memory pools with weaker ECC, longer refresh and lower-bin dies.
why: Cost per bit and supply: creates demand for lower-reliability bits that existing fabs can produce with relaxed test and repair, raising sellable yield without new capacity.

title: Reworkable HBM: low-melt indium bumps let bad dies be swapped
idea: Rule: an HBM stack must be repairable at die level. Core dies are stacked with indium or Sn-Bi microbumps that reflow at ~120-140 C instead of permanent hybrid bonds, so a die that fails at stack test or in the field can be desoldered and replaced at a repair station.
why: Fact 6: much of the 20-30% HBM stack yield loss becomes a die swap rather than scrapping 8-12 good dies.

title: Self-clearing capacitor electrodes borrowed from metallized-film power capacitors
idea: Combine the self-healing of metallized-film capacitors with DRAM MIM capacitors: an ALD ZrO2/Al2O3 dielectric under a 5-10 nm sputtered Al (or TiN/Al) top electrode thin enough that a breakdown spot's discharge vaporizes or oxidizes the electrode locally, isolating the defect while the cell keeps working at slightly lower C. Buildable in a university nanofab: ALD, sputter and lift-off only.
why: Dielectric weak-spot leakage and yield: converts leaky or shorted cells into working ones, permitting thinner, higher-C dielectrics (fact 1) with fewer failures.

title: Per-tier Seebeck thermopiles let 100-tier stacks refresh by tier
idea: Effect: Seebeck thermoelectric voltage. In a ~100-tier 3D DRAM whose inner tiers run 10-20 K hotter than outer ones, thermocouple pairs formed in the staircase contacts read each tier's temperature with zero bias power; the controller assigns per-tier refresh intervals (cool tiers ~4x longer) and steers hot data to cool tiers.
why: 10x density: without per-tier refresh the hottest tier sets refresh for all 100, a 30-40% bandwidth tax at 3D densities; keeping it under 10% makes a ~100-tier (~10x) stack viable, with thermocouples added to existing staircase steps at near-zero cost.
